Livermore School Board · Seat 5 · Nov 3, 2026
# Let's get down to business.
I'm Sam Phelps — a father, not a politician. Our kids deserve a board that answers to them. Livermore graduates 97% of its students, but the state's own numbers show our most vulnerable kids sliding backward — and almost nobody is talking about it. I intend to.
Tell me what's on your mind Where I stand
My two opponents both already sit on this board, with terms running through 2028.
97% of our kids graduate. Barely half finish the courses UC and CSU require. Let's talk about that.
Why this is personal
## The future is watching every move I make.
I have a teenager at Livermore High right now. I have two little ones who will walk into these same schools in a few years. Whatever this board decides, my family lives inside the result of it — not for one election cycle, but for the next fifteen years.
That's my stake in this. Every decision this board makes, my family lives with — same as yours.
1 at Livermore High today 2 more headed there 15 years of this district ahead of us
## The numbers we need to talk about.
These are the state's own figures, most recent year available. Not opinions, not spin — the same reports the board reads and files away.
52.9%
Dublin 80.9% · Pleasanton 80.8%
Share of Livermore graduates who finished the courses UC and CSU require for admission.
5.9%
Alameda County average: 10.9%
Livermore English learners meeting the state math standard — barely half the county rate.
−4.6
Reading −4.3 · district math flat
Points Livermore's Latino students have lost on the state math test since 2019. District-wide over those same years, math held flat and reading slipped about a point.
Sources — check every number yourself.
UC/CSU (A–G) completion, 2024–25. CDE DataQuest, Four-Year Adjusted Cohort Graduation Rate: Livermore · Dublin · Pleasanton. The report opens on counts — switch Display Options to “Percents.” Livermore 553 of 1,045 graduates (52.9%), Dublin 691 of 854 (80.9%), Pleasanton 932 of 1,153 (80.8%); the denominator is graduates. The rates are also printed directly in CDE’s downloadable file. This is A–G completion, which is a different measure from the Dashboard College/Career Indicator.
State test results. CAASPP research files for Alameda County: 2024–25 and 2018–19, with the student-group key. Filter to district 01-61200, school code 0000000, all grades, “Percentage Standard Met and Above.” English learners are group 160 (5.85% Livermore vs 10.90% county in math); Latino students are group 78 (math 31.43% → 26.88%, reading 44.60% → 40.33%).
What I'd do about it
Where I stand
## Three things I will fight for.
Not twelve. Three. A board member who promises everything delivers nothing.
01
### Every kid — not just the ones who were already going to be fine.
Livermore graduates 97% of its students. That's real and I'll say so. But barely half of those graduates — 52.9% — finished the courses UC and CSU require. In Dublin and Pleasanton it's about 81%. A diploma should open doors — for too many of our kids, it doesn't.
Underneath that, our Latino students have lost more than four points on state tests since 2019, while district-wide math held flat and reading slipped about a point. And here's the one that keeps me up: our English learners score worse in math than in reading. In Dublin they run fourteen points better in math, in Pleasanton nearly ten. Livermore is the only Tri-Valley district where it runs backward — and it has every year since 2019. Math is the less language-loaded subject. That is not a poverty problem you can shrug at. That is an instruction problem, and it is fixable.
I want every board meeting to open with the same question: what did we do this month for the kids furthest behind?
02
### Spend it in the classroom, or don't spend it.
On February 6, this board agreed to pay a departing superintendent $364,000 — a full year's salary — in a separation agreement. Eighteen days later, it approved a $14.8 million budget-reduction plan. In June it put about $2.7 million of that back.
Livermore is now on its fourth superintendent in four years, and the district went from a positive budget certification to a qualified one inside a single year. Whatever the reasons — and some were outside anyone's control — the pattern is the same: churn at the top, cuts closest to the kids.
I'm not going to pretend a school board can conjure money. I am going to ask, out loud, at every single meeting: does this dollar reach a classroom? If the answer is no, it needs a very good reason.
03
### Decide it in public, or don't decide it.
In January, a proposal to close two elementary schools surfaced in the agenda for the January 13 board meeting — it wasn't in the draft emailed to families eleven days earlier — with a final vote on cuts then set for February 10. One week later, the board unanimously took closures off the table. Then on February 7, a superintendent separation was announced by press release on a Saturday morning — and no vote was announced when the board met the night before. It took three days and a reporter's question to learn the board had voted 4–0, with one abstention.
Board President Steven Drouin acknowledged it himself that January — "we've had trust issues with the community" — and to his credit, the board moved its meetings to the evening so working parents could actually attend. That was the right call. The next step is making that openness the habit, not the exception.
Parents here aren't asking to run the district. They're asking to find out before it's decided. Real notice. Plain-English numbers posted before the vote, not after. And a roll call on every consequential decision, every time.
About Sam
## Why I'm running.
I graduated from Amador Valley High, gave college a shot, and figured out fast it wasn't for me — so I went to work. Fifteen years in construction later, I'm a project manager for a mid-size general contractor: tight, budget-conscious work where a quarter inch and a few thousand dollars both matter, and somebody is accountable when either goes wrong. That somebody is usually me. I also run RSVP, a direct-mail company serving contractors, restaurants, and small businesses around this valley — the people who actually hire this district's graduates. And I've had a teacher at my kitchen table for seven years: my fiancée taught fifth grade before stepping out of the classroom to raise our two youngest.
I've got a daughter at Livermore High right now and two little ones who'll be walking into these schools before I know it. I want a hand on the wheel while they're in it. And to be clear about where I stand: I'm not saying every kid belongs in college — I came up in the trades, and I'll take a good framer over a lot of degrees. I'm saying every kid should get to choose — and right now we're closing that door on nearly half of them before they ever walk out of it.
Both of my opponents are sitting trustees. I'm the only candidate for Seat 5 who isn't already on this board — and what I bring instead is fifteen years of pricing jobs. When a number comes across the table, I know whether it's real, whether it's padded, and whether it buys what it says it buys. Every budget has fluff and every budget has foundation; the job is cutting one without touching the other. And when the bids come in, I'd rather walk the site than sit through the presentation about it.
I'm not running against two people. I'm running against the idea that a 97% graduation rate means the job is done.
— Sam
What's on your mind
## You talk. I'll listen.
A class your kid can't get into. A board decision that made no sense. Something this district gets right that nobody says out loud. Whatever it is — that's exactly what I want to hear before November, not after.
#### Prefer email?
sam@bayarearsvp.com — same inbox, same guy.
#### Check your area
Not sure if Seat 5 covers your address? It's "Trustee Area 5" on the district's official map, on the elections page.
#### Register or check your registration
Ballots were mailed October 5 — you can vote now. Register online by Monday, October 19 at registertovote.ca.gov. Missed it? You can still register and vote the same day at the Registrar's office or any Alameda County vote center through 8 p.m. on Election Day, Tuesday, November 3, 2026.
